title: Change the tissue to improve particle delivery
subtitle: Tumor endothelium · Extracellular matrix
challenge: The tissue environment can limit how nanoparticles distribute inside a tumor, even after particles reach its blood vessels.
idea: Test whether vascular normalization could improve delivery of 100 nm particles—even though tumor accumulation is often attributed to leaky vessels.
approach: Tumor endothelial cell-targeted liposomal siRNA inhibited VEGFR2. The study examined vascular maturation, intratumoral particle distribution and mechanisms involving matrix remodeling.
outcome: Particle distribution and treatment efficacy improved despite vascular maturation in the preclinical study. Inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases or depleting macrophages removed the distribution benefit.
contribution: Developed the hypothesis that vascular normalization could improve particle delivery, and investigated the underlying mechanism; first author of the matrix-remodeling study.
relevance: Investigate a biological barrier as a modifiable part of the delivery system, and use mechanistic experiments to test the explanation.
evidenceNote: Published preclinical findings. Individual attribution is supported by Sakurai's first-person 2022 award review (Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin, DOI 10.1248/bpb.b22-00317), especially section 5, which explicitly describes his hypothesis and development of the vascular-normalization strategy. First authorship of the 2016 matrix-remodeling paper is independently verified. No sole-inventor claim is made.
teamValue: Expand the design choices for delivery by addressing tissue biology as well as particle composition.

researchFigure.alt: Published graphical abstract: cyclic RGD-modified siRNA particles targeting VEGFR2 are shown beside tumor sections before and after treatment. The tumor-vessel-type renal carcinoma and stroma-vessel-type colorectal models show different particle distribution responses.
researchFigure.takeaway: Compare the upper and lower panels: VEGFR2 silencing improved particle distribution in tumor-vessel-type models; the stroma-vessel-type model did not show the same benefit.
researchFigure.context: Figure from the 2017 follow-up study. The matrix-remodeling result and my contribution in this case refer to the 2016 study. Both are preclinical.
researchFigure.credit: Source: Yamamoto, Kato, Sakurai et al. · Journal of Controlled Release · 2017

hook.label: VASCULAR NORMALIZATION
hook.question: Could more mature vessels improve delivery?
hook.evidence: VEGFR2-targeted siRNA improved nanoparticle delivery in preclinical tumors. Mechanistic experiments implicated remodeling of the surrounding matrix.
hook.skill: Treat tissue biology as a design variable.

title: Test a transcellular route into tumors
subtitle: Caveolin-1 · Transcytosis · EPR-related delivery
challenge: VEGFR2 silencing increased liposome accumulation despite vascular maturation in a renal cell carcinoma model. The mechanism needed an explanation.
idea: Test a route through endothelial cells involving Caveolin-1, alongside the conventional model of transport through gaps between cells.
approach: Co-suppress Caveolin-1 and VEGFR2 using endothelial-targeted siRNA, then assess liposome accumulation and vascular structure.
outcome: Caveolin-1 knockdown cancelled the delivery increase associated with VEGFR2 silencing without changing vascular structure, supporting involvement of a transcellular route in this model.
contribution: First author of the Caveolin-1 study, with Akari Kato and Hideyoshi Harashima.
relevance: Distinguish alternative explanations with a mechanistic perturbation.
teamValue: Design experiments that separate competing delivery mechanisms.
evidenceNote: The primary paper reports Caveolin-1 co-silencing in a renal cell carcinoma model. The effect supports involvement of a transcellular mechanism in this setting; it does not establish a universal explanation for the EPR effect. First authorship is verified. No historical priority or sole-inventor claim is made.

hook.label: TRANSCYTOSIS & THE EPR EFFECT
hook.question: Could active transport help explain tumor delivery?
hook.evidence: Caveolin-1 perturbation supported a transcellular contribution to liposome accumulation in a renal tumor model.
hook.skill: Test an alternative to the prevailing explanation.

title: Discover an unexpected route into lymphatic endothelium
subtitle: Targeted LNPs · Lymphatic endothelium
challenge: LNP uptake through ApoE is commonly associated with liver delivery. The challenge was to deliver siRNA to lymphatic endothelial cells.
idea: Connect two clues: ApoE is present in lymph, and lymphatic endothelial cells express LDLR. Could a mechanism associated with liver uptake open a route into these cells?
approach: The ApoE–LDLR hypothesis guided tests of ApoE-dependent LNP uptake. Subcutaneous delivery and a dense coating of short-chain PEG lipids then enabled evaluation in vivo.
outcome: The study demonstrated ApoE-dependent uptake into lymphatic endothelial cells. Optimized siRNA-LNPs reduced VEGFR3 expression in vivo in preclinical experiments.
contribution: Conceived and experimentally validated the ApoE-mediated lymphatic delivery concept with collaborators; first author of the study.
relevance: Generate an unexpected mechanistic hypothesis, test it, and turn the finding into a strategy for extrahepatic delivery.
relatedInsight: A complementary approach used CLIP chemistry to attach targeting antibodies to LNPs. Anti-podoplanin LNPs demonstrated lymphatic endothelial delivery in vitro and in vivo.

evidenceFlow.label: HYPOTHESIS
evidenceFlow.title: ApoE in lymph + LDLR on target cells
evidenceFlow.text: A possible route into lymphatic endothelium, inspired by liver uptake.

evidenceFlow.label: CELL EVIDENCE
evidenceFlow.title: ApoE-dependent LNP uptake
evidenceFlow.text: Demonstrated in cultured lymphatic endothelial cells.

evidenceFlow.label: IN VIVO EVIDENCE
evidenceFlow.title: VEGFR3 silencing
evidenceFlow.text: After subcutaneous delivery of optimized siRNA-LNPs in a preclinical model.

evidenceNote: The user directly identified conceiving, discovering and experimentally validating the ApoE-mediated lymphatic delivery route as a personal contribution. First authorship and study-level findings are independently supported by PubMed. No sole-inventor or universal historical-priority claim is made; LDLR is described as part of the hypothesis, and PEG-lipid release is not presented as a proven mechanism.
teamValue: Generate and test targeting hypotheses for cell populations that are difficult to reach.

researchFigure.alt: Published graphical abstract: PEG-rich siRNA lipid nanoparticles move from the subcutis into lymph, followed by proposed PEG-lipid detachment, ApoE association and uptake by lymphatic endothelial cells. A bar chart compares uptake at three PEG-DMG levels.
researchFigure.takeaway: Follow the route from the injection site into lymph: particle design enables transport, then ApoE supports uptake by lymphatic endothelial cells.
researchFigure.context: The graphic summarizes the proposed route. ApoE-dependent uptake was tested experimentally; PEG-lipid detachment remains a proposed step.
researchFigure.credit: Source: Sakurai et al. · Journal of Controlled Release · 2023

hook.label: A NEW TARGET CELL
hook.question: Could a familiar uptake mechanism reach a new cell type?
hook.evidence: An ApoE-mediated uptake hypothesis led to siRNA delivery to lymphatic endothelial cells and in vivo VEGFR3 silencing.
hook.skill: Transfer a biological insight to a new context.

title: Use DoE to optimize sentinel-node selectivity
subtitle: Lymphatic imaging · Design of Experiments
challenge: A sentinel-node probe needs to accumulate in the first draining node with limited spread to downstream nodes.
idea: Combine transport, macrophage uptake and the injection environment in the formulation strategy, then optimize the lipid composition systematically.
approach: A five-factor, two-level design tested 16 conditions covering phospholipid, sterol, PEG-lipid content, filter size and hyaluronidase. Follow-up experiments varied phosphatidylserine content and compared sentinel-node imaging with indocyanine green.
outcome: The studies reported improved sentinel-node detection with hyaluronidase and greater sentinel-node selectivity of the optimized particles than indocyanine green in preclinical models.
contribution: Co-first and co-corresponding author of the DoE study; contributed to conceptualization, experiments, data curation, visualization and writing.
relevance: Define the biological performance objective, study its determinants, and use DoE to guide formulation choices.
evidenceNote: The full article confirms a five-factor, two-level, 16-condition design in Methods 2.6 and Table 1; a contradictory phrase in the introduction is not used. The 2.8-fold comparison is from a separate PS-content experiment (Results 3.3/Figure 3), not from the 16-condition screen. Author notes establish equal first contribution and shared correspondence; the contributions section credits Yu Sakurai with conceptualization, investigation, data curation, visualization and writing. Formal analysis is credited to Hidetaka Akita and is not assigned to Sakurai.
teamValue: Translate a biological delivery objective into formulation criteria and informative experiments.
quantitativeEvidence: In a follow-up mouse experiment, 30% phosphatidylserine liposomes gave 2.8-fold greater sentinel-node selectivity than PS-free liposomes. Selectivity was the sentinel-to-axillary-node accumulation ratio (n = 3 per condition; Figure 3).

researchFigure.alt: Published graphical abstract: medium-sized negatively charged liposomes are retained in the first draining lymph node through macrophage uptake, with less signal in the next node. A lower panel illustrates sentinel-node mapping from a tumor.
researchFigure.takeaway: Keep the signal in the first draining lymph node: liposome size and negative surface charge favor macrophage uptake and local retention.
researchFigure.context: Figure from the mechanistic imaging study in Molecular Therapy (2021). The DoE optimization in this case was reported separately in Pharmaceutics (2021).
researchFigure.credit: Source: Gomi, Sakurai et al. · Molecular Therapy · 2021
